move: Marks off a 'region of human liberty' — conduct affecting only oneself or others by their consent — over which society has no legitimate interest, listing conscience, opinion, and choice of life-plan as immune from interference.
States the harm principle outright: self-protection is the sole warrant for coercing anyone, and the agent's own physical or moral good is explicitly denied as sufficient warrant.

Extends the principle to a hard case, conceding that soliciting another is a social rather than self-regarding act but concluding the grounds of individual liberty still cover free consultation and advice.
Qualifies the principle by endorsing an exception in which a person is released from an engagement because it is injurious to himself, citing the voiding of contracts of self-enslavement.

Applies the harm criterion against prevailing sentiment, arguing that acts producing wretched offspring are injurious to others and so restrainable, while purely self-pleasing conduct is wrongly restricted.

Presses the paternalist objection that if protection against themselves is owed to children, it is owed to adults incapable of self-government, so law and opinion should repress gambling, drunkenness, and idleness.
Argues that cultivating individuality is what produces well-developed human beings and benefits even those who do not want liberty, without addressing what may limit liberty.

Delimits which controls are questions of liberty at all, granting that anti-adulteration and workplace-safety regulation is undeniable in principle while objecting to restrictions on obtaining commodities as infringements on the buyer.
Voices the objection that the self-regarding/other-regarding distinction is untenable, since harm to oneself always reaches connections, drains common resources, and corrupts by example.
Locates the real difficulty not in drawing the boundary but in the majority's indifference to individual spontaneity as an intrinsic good, leaving the criterion for limiting liberty unaddressed.
Applies the harm criterion to the family: a person is free in his own concerns but not when acting for another, so the state must vigilantly control power exercised over wives and dependents.
Illustrates the general principle of liberty by holding a person morally responsible for failing to weigh the interests of others his step would affect.
